resources.string: Noise reduction, sharpening, tone and the frame merge

Scales the finished photo down to this size, keeping the frame\'s proportions. If the chosen size is not smaller than the merged one, the photo stays as it is. For 16 or 20 MP from a 12 MP sensor set Resolution to 1.5× or 2×.
Megapixels of the photo, e.g. 24 or 8.5
Width x height the photo fits in (4000x3000), or its long side (4000)
How many pixels the photo gets. 2× gives more detail but takes about four times longer to process.

How the camera builds a photo from its burst. Fast: the photo is ready noticeably sooner. Quality: slower, but motion, water and fine detail come out cleaner. Static: for still scenes on a tripod or a steady hand; slower again, finer detail; it leaves moving frames and areas out by itself. Every mode always makes the photo its own way and never hands it to another, on any sensor (Quad, Tetra, DCG) and through GPU failures.
What removes the colour fringe on contrasty edges beside a bright light. The network cleans edges better and leaves the real colour of things alone. Classic is the earlier method.
The photo\'s tone: brightness, local contrast, curve and colour. V1 is the tone as before, V2 the new version. Its settings: “Tone settings” below.
The Why tone\'s tone mapping: exposure, global and local tone mapping, the highlight shoulder and the tone\'s highlights. Rows of one version only are greyed while the other is chosen.
Fine tuning of the network that removes colour fringes: how strongly it works and which fringes it treats as a defect.
How much of the network\'s correction goes into the photo. At zero the fringe stays as it is.
Wide removes a fringe up to 12 pixels from a bright edge, such as window frames against the sky. Narrow is a little faster.
From which hue a fringe counts as a defect. Lower: bluish fringes go too. Higher: only violet and magenta ones.
How much brighter the light nearby
A fringe is removed only beside a light this many times brighter than it. The higher the value, the fewer places are touched.
How bright the light beside a fringe has to be, as a share of white. Lower: fringes beside dimmer lights go too.
Also removes the green fringe. It appears on the edges of things that are out of focus.
Keep the glow of coloured lights
Coloured lamps, LEDs and signs keep their glow: the network does not take it for a fringe.
Where the network removes a fringe, the classic method\'s result is taken instead if it removed more.
The correction can only weaken a fringe\'s colour. It never turns it into the opposite colour.
The method that scales the finished frame down to the chosen size. Lanczos gives a sharper result, Bilinear is faster.
Short frames for the highlights, long ones for the shadows: when, how many, how they blend

How many frames are merged into one photo. Higher: less noise and more detail even at night, but slower shooting and processing. Lower: a quick release for children and motion. The frames come from the buffer; if it holds fewer, that many are merged. 50 and 200 MP have rows of their own.
On: frames taken before the press are used, plus extra ones after it. Off: the whole burst is taken after the press.
How many frames to take and merge for a 50 MP shot. At zero the same as «Frames in the burst». At most 65. If memory runs short the burst is shorter, and the camera says so.

How many frames to take and merge for a 200 MP shot, from 3 to 64. The last frame is very short, for the highlights; the rest are ordinary. 4 by default. If memory runs short the burst is shorter, and the camera says so.
An extra very dark frame rescues blown areas such as lamps and the sky. Auto takes it only when the frame has blown areas.
How many dark frames to take. Higher: less noise in the highlights, but slightly longer shooting.
How strictly dark frames are checked for motion. Stricter: fewer dark silhouettes of hands against lamps.

Guards against doubled headlights and street lamps when shooting handheld. Lower: a strict choice, and at the slightest shake the base frame is kept without doubled lights. At 100 rejection is off and the short frame is always merged.
Highlight frames: how many times shorter than N
How many times darker the dark frame is than an ordinary one. Higher: rescues brighter lamps, but noisier. Lower: the other way round.
Highlight frames: clipping threshold for Auto
For Auto: at what share of blown pixels the dark frame is taken. Higher: less often. Lower: more often.
Extra bright frames after the press: less noise in the shadows. Off: faster shooting with no risk of blur.
When a bright frame is dropped. Auto: if it is blurred. Always: only if there was motion in the frame.
Shadow frames: drop on motion, % of the frame
For Always: how much motion a bright frame may have. Higher: it is used more often. Lower: less often.
How many bright frames to take. Higher: cleaner shadows, but longer shooting and more memory.
How much brighter the bright frames are than ordinary ones, in stops. Higher: cleaner shadows, but each frame is noisier. Lower: the other way round.
A correction of the noise in bright places by which the merge tells noise from motion. Higher: a smoother picture, but ghosts may appear. Lower: sharper and noisier.
The same correction for dark places. Higher: smoother shadows, but ghosts may appear. Lower: sharper and noisier.
How the burst\'s frames are aligned and added into one, and how the noise is cleaned after the merge. Rows the chosen processing mode does not use are greyed.
What aligns the burst\'s frames: the system module (vivo only) or the one built into the app.

Where the precise frame matching is computed. Auto: on the CPU alongside the merge when possible, otherwise on the GPU before the merge. GPU: always on the GPU, leaving the CPU free. The result is the same.
Precise matching of the frames area by area. It gives more detail when shooting handheld and adds about 0.8 seconds of processing.
How ghosts of moving objects are removed
How strictly the merge rejects what moves. Higher: no ghosts of passing people and cars, but a noisier shot. Lower: more frames go into the merge, with possible ghosts.
How much of the difference between frames to count as noise. Higher: fewer still areas are mistaken for motion and more frames are merged. Lower: stricter toward motion.
The safety zone round moving things. Lower: a wider zone with no halos where they meet the background. Higher: a narrower zone, closer to the outline.
Weak rejection below this threshold counts as noise and does not spread to nearby places. Higher: cleaner. Lower: fewer ghosts.
Removes ghosts harder where parts of the frame move differently, such as hands or leaves. Works together with area-by-area frame matching.
How textured an area must be for the stronger motion rejection to start. Higher: only on clearly contrasty objects. Lower: even on low-contrast areas.
From which spread of motion the stronger rejection starts. Lower: fewer ghosts. Higher: less noise.
How the frames blend into pixels: sharpness versus noise
A new way of blending the frames: more detail at night and handheld. Off: the earlier kernel.

Up to which light level a shot counts as a night shot. The merge\'s night noise settings depend on it, and in Auto so does the new kernel. Higher: brighter scenes count as night too. It does not affect 200 MP shots at 4×: those are taken in daylight.
New kernel by day: hand shake from, px
In daylight on Auto with precise frame matching: from how much hand shake the new kernel turns on. Lower: more often (a tripod shot gets noisier). Higher: less often.
How wide the frame blending is. Higher: softer and cleaner. Lower: sharper but noisier.
The size of the blending spot on ordinary textured surfaces such as sand, asphalt and leaves. Higher: smoother, cleaner surfaces. Lower: crisper micro-texture with more grain. 1 is as before.

The size of the blending spot in out-of-focus areas and bokeh: the sky, walls, a blurred background. Higher: the background blurs softer and cleaner, without grain. Lower: fine grain stays. 1 is as before.
From which level of detail an area counts as flat and gets the bokeh kernel. Higher: more of the frame counts as flat and the picture is smoother. Lower: more of it counts as texture. 1 is as before.
Noise scale for the SNR key
For the earlier kernel only: how noisy to take the shot to be. Higher: softer and cleaner. Lower: sharper and noisier.
For the earlier kernel only: how much noise not to take for edges. Higher: smoother flat areas. Lower: sharper.

Where motion left little more than the base frame, it is softened so that moving objects have no noise round them. Higher: cleaner but softer. Lower: sharper. The native Quad and Tetra merge has its own rule, and Sport mode always uses 0.
Removes the coloured zigzag on the edges of moving objects. Higher: stronger. Zero turns it off. It does nothing in the native Quad and Tetra merge.
Keeps colour from running along thin lines while the coloured zigzag is removed. It does nothing in the native Quad and Tetra merge.
The largest weight a bright frame gets in the merge. Higher: cleaner shadows. Lower: bright frames count for less.
How much more bright frames weigh than ordinary ones. Higher: cleaner shadows. Lower: their share is closer to ordinary frames.
Blurs very bright shadow frames. Higher: less noise in the shadows, but less detail too. One turns it off. It works in dark scenes where the bright frame comes from a long shutter.

The merge for cameras that deliver a Quad 2×2 or Tetra 4×4 mosaic frame: the merge method and its settings. In Fast the fast merge takes Quad - the method and kernel here act on Tetra; in Static the Quality merge takes Quad and Tetra.
These rows are for cameras whose frame arrives as a Quad 2×2 or Tetra 4×4 mosaic.

On: the Quad or Tetra mosaic is assembled by the merge into an ordinary full-resolution frame. Off: the frames are merged without that and only a DNG is saved, the merged mosaic to develop in Scam Remosaic or another app.
Frames in the mosaic merge: at most
The most mosaic frames in the merge (the shot\'s overall frame count applies first). Higher: less noise but slower. Lower: faster but noisier.
Only with sub-frame splitting and the new kernel: the sharpness on edges. Lower: sharper but grainier. Higher: softer.
How the mosaic is merged. Native is faster and more detailed; splitting into sub-frames is the earlier way.

The radius of the area the dots are taken from. Higher: less noise but slower. Lower: faster but noisier. For Quad and Tetra T2, 1 to 3 use the fast merge and 4 the general one, which is slower. Tetra T1\'s window is twice as wide.
Takes the whole square area round a dot: less noise on flat areas. Off: the window is as with splitting, and the merge goes the general way.
The blending width of the native Quad and Tetra T2 merge in daylight. Lower: sharper but noisier. Higher: softer and cleaner. At night and for Tetra T1 the merge uses its own tuned values.
The sharpness on edges in the native merge. Lower: sharper, but below 0.5 edges take on colour. Higher: softer. Works with the new merge kernel; at night the merge uses its own value.
How much flat areas are smoothed in the native merge. Higher: less noise. Lower: grainier. Works with the new merge kernel.
Limits how narrow the blending can get, which protects edges from teeth and colour fringes.
The sharpness of the green channel on mosaic sensors. Higher: the most sharpness and detail, but noisier. Lower: softer and more reliable.
Fights colour moiré on mosaic sensors. Lower: the colour grid and moiré go, with softer colour. Higher: sharper red and blue, with more false colour.
Fills in red and blue where there are few dots, so the colour of fine detail does not drop out. It helps with few frames, but with many it can tint edges.
When the colour recovery starts. Higher: more often. Lower: only when data is really short. Works only with the recovery on.
How the Tetra 4×4 mosaic is merged. T1 is more detailed and faster; the others are earlier ways.

How smoothly the dark frames come in at blown areas. At zero the transition is the sharpest; higher makes the edge of the area where they replace the base frames softer. Separate bright objects are not affected.

For the native Quad and Tetra merge only: how much the dark frame is blurred in the highlights. Higher: softer lights. Below 0.7 coloured teeth appear on the edges. On an ordinary sensor the softness is set by «Highlight frames: soft transition».
Highlight frames: highlight edge colour, σ px

Smooths the colour of the short frames at the edges of blown areas. Higher: more even colour. Lower: a coloured dotted line. For the ordinary merge only; it does nothing in the native Quad and Tetra merge.
For Auto: how sharp a bright frame has to be. Higher: blurred ones are dropped more often. Lower: less often.
For Auto: how many times brighter than an ordinary frame a bright one may be. Higher: brighter ones are allowed. Lower: stricter.
Overexposed areas and stray coloured dots

Protects against purple fringes round lamps and blown areas, but also throws out dark dots next to the light from every frame, so edges against bright light come out jagged. Off by default: the merge clips blown areas dot by dot.

How far a dot has to stand out from its neighbours to count as a hot pixel, a coloured speck on night shots. Lower: faint defects go too, but detail may suffer. Higher: only bright white dots. Zero turns it off.
The same for random spikes in the base frame. Lower: more is removed. Zero turns it off.
Up to which light level hot pixels are looked for. Higher: in brighter scenes too. Lower: only at dusk and at night, so daytime micro-texture stays untouched.
Checks the dark frame more strictly and skips it if it would spoil the photo. Off: the earlier checks apply.
Matching colour and brightness of bright frames to the main one
Before the merge, matches the colour and brightness of bright frames to the base one so the photo has no colour shifts.
Turns every denoiser on. Off: only the frame merge is left, and the photo is grainier but more detailed.
The final clean-up of leftover noise after the merge. Higher: noise goes completely at the cost of slight smoothing. At zero the filter is off and the merge\'s own result stays.

The balance between the merge\'s raw sharpness and the denoiser\'s smoothness in still areas. Higher: fine detail stays crisp, as after the merge, with natural grain. Lower: a smooth, noiseless picture.
How much of its own sharpness is kept where motion left few frames to merge. Higher: a moving subject stays crisp, with its natural noise. Lower: the denoiser smooths it more.
Brings back a fine natural texture where few frames were merged, so things do not look like plasticine. Higher: a more textured photo, as from a big camera. At zero the image is perfectly smooth.
How much harder areas made from few frames are cleaned (lamps, motion). Higher: cleaner; lower: more detail.
How the camera estimates the noise of the shot
Correction of the auto SNR. Higher: the shot is treated as brighter and cleaner; lower: darker and noisier.
Noise model correction for mid and bright tones. Higher: stronger smoothing; lower: more detail.
Noise model correction for the shadows. Higher: smoother shadows; lower: more detail and grain in shadows.
Strength multipliers of the multiscale denoiser by scene and for colour; the overall luma strength is “Noise reduction” in the “Picture” group
How much the brightness noise (grain) is smoothed. Higher: smoother; lower: more grain and detail; 0: off. Details: “Noise reduction: details” (For experts › SHDR).
Luma denoise strength at night, in dim and in normal light. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Luma denoise strength at dusk and in bright light. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Overall colour denoise strength. Higher: fewer colour blotches; lower: more accurate colour; 0: off.
How much fine grain is put back after denoising. Higher: sharper and grainier; lower: smoother.
Extra denoiser tweaks; the base denoiser by default
Limit of the grain put back, matters at night. 1: never more grain than the shot had (default); above 1 the grain is amplified; 0: none.
Cleaning of large luma blotches. Higher: fewer blotches but washed-out texture; 0: texture is left alone.
Minimum colour denoise strength in any light. Higher: smoother colour even in daylight; 0: no minimum.
2× grid and 200 MP shots: share of fine colour kept. Higher: more colour detail and colour noise; lower: cleaner colour.
Fade colour in the darkest areas
Removes the colour tint in near-black areas: the darkest pixels become neutral.
Luma denoise values for each light level
Night point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Night: luma denoise strength, 5 numbers fine to coarse grain. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Night: grain put back, 5 numbers fine to coarse. Higher: sharper, grainier; lower: smoother.
Night: luma smoothing reach, 5 numbers 0–1. Higher: smoother but softer edges; lower: crisper edges.
Dusk point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Dusk: luma denoise strength, 5 numbers fine to coarse grain. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Dusk: grain put back, 5 numbers fine to coarse. Higher: sharper, grainier; lower: smoother.
Dusk: luma smoothing reach, 5 numbers 0–1. Higher: smoother but softer edges; lower: crisper edges.
Dim light point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Dim light: luma denoise strength, 5 numbers fine to coarse grain. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Dim light: grain put back, 5 numbers fine to coarse. Higher: sharper, grainier; lower: smoother.
Dim light: luma smoothing reach, 5 numbers 0–1. Higher: smoother but softer edges; lower: crisper edges.
Normal light point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Normal light: luma denoise strength, 5 numbers fine to coarse grain. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Normal light: grain put back, 5 numbers fine to coarse. Higher: sharper, grainier; lower: smoother.
Normal light: luma smoothing reach, 5 numbers 0–1. Higher: smoother but softer edges; lower: crisper edges.
Bright light point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Bright light: luma denoise strength, 5 numbers fine to coarse grain. Higher: smoother; lower: more detail.
Bright light: grain put back, 5 numbers fine to coarse. Higher: sharper, grainier; lower: smoother.
Bright light: luma smoothing reach, 5 numbers 0–1. Higher: smoother but softer edges; lower: crisper edges.
Colour denoise values for each light level
Deep night point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Deep night: colour smoothing reach, 5 integers 0–16. Higher: smoother but colour bleeds; lower: crisper.
Night point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Night: colour smoothing reach, 5 integers 0–16. Higher: smoother but colour bleeds; lower: crisper.
Dusk point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Dusk: colour smoothing reach, 5 integers 0–16. Higher: smoother but colour bleeds; lower: crisper.
Dim light point: the SNR where it applies. Higher: used on brighter shots; lower: on darker ones.
Dim light: colour smoothing reach, 5 integers 0–16. Higher: smoother but colour bleeds; lower: crisper.
The detailed sharpening settings: the unsharp mask, edges, local contrast and protection of shadows and highlights from oversharpening.
This is the photo\'s only sharpening; it works on brightness before the tone processing. Its overall strength is «Sharpness» on the main page, and the rows here weaken or boost its separate parts.
How much fine detail goes into the photo. Higher: sharper and crisper. Lower: softer. At zero no extra sharpening. The detailed settings are on the Sharpness page.
The brightness the sharpening is computed on. «After exposure»: in dark scenes the sharpening is weaker on strong edges.
The scale of every sharpening radius. At zero it is chosen by the photo\'s size. Higher: coarser sharpening. Lower: finer.
The size of the detail the unsharp mask brings out. Lower: micro-texture such as pores, fabric, sand. Higher: large outlines and object borders, with more visible halos. Zero turns it off.
Brightness steps below this threshold count as noise and are not sharpened. Higher: flat areas stay clean, without grain. At zero sharpening is strongest, but noise is sharpened too.
The size of the detail boosted by the edge-preserving sharpening. Higher: larger detail is caught. Lower: the finest sharpening. Zero turns it off.
How much the texture of objects is boosted without halos at borders. Higher: more relief, but more noise too. Lower: a soft, smooth texture. Zero turns it off.
Which brightness step counts as a border that must not be blurred. Higher: larger steps are boosted too. Lower: the filter stops strictly at any contrasty seam.
The scale at which the photo is split into shape and relief. Higher: large folds and structures stand out. Lower: the fine texture grid. Zero turns it off.

How carefully the filter treats edges, in thousandths. Lower: it follows outlines closely without halos and boosts only faint texture. Higher: it acts like an ordinary soft blur and touches visible edges too.
How much the hidden texture of stone, wood, fabric and skin shows. Higher: tangible volume and micro-contrast. Lower: a calm, natural texture. Below zero the texture is smoothed.
Adds fine film grain, strongest in the mid-tones. Higher: more visible grain that hides digital noise. At zero the picture is smooth.
Restoring the lens\'s sharpness in three stages, from diffraction to fine texture, with halo protection.
Removes the dark and light fringes that appear round contrasty borders when sharpness is restored. Higher: a clean result without fringes. Lower: harder restoration.
How much fine contrast is allowed before the halo protection steps in. Higher: the finest strokes are restored without clipping. Lower: borders are held more strictly.
The local contrast above which the restoration fades out. Higher: it works even on sharp, contrasty seams, with possible halos. Lower: only on fine, faint texture.
The shape of the blur the first stage corrects. Gaussian: light scattered in the lens. Disc: slight smear and defocus. Airy: the diffraction of a phone\'s small optics.
The radius of the lens\'s blur spot, in pixels. Higher: corrects strong defocus and mush, with possible halos. Lower: fine tuning of small detail. Zero turns the stage off.
The shape of the blur corrected by the second stage: medium detail and defocus. Gaussian: scattered light. Disc: smear and defocus. Airy: diffraction.
The radius of the blur spot for this stage, in pixels. Higher: corrects larger blur. Lower: finer. Zero turns the stage off.
The shape of the blur corrected by the third stage: fine texture. Gaussian: scattered light. Disc: smear and defocus. Airy: diffraction.
The radius of the blur spot for this stage, in pixels. Higher: corrects larger blur. Lower: finer. Zero turns the stage off.
Gently weakens sharpening in deep shadows so that noise does not show. Higher: cleaner shadows. At zero shadows are sharpened like the rest of the frame.
Gently weakens sharpening in bright highlights. Higher: no harsh traces or spiky halos round lamps and glints. Lower: glints are sharpened like the rest of the frame.
Removes the light fringe along contrasty borders such as wires against the sky or branches. Higher: fewer halos, less visible sharpening. Lower: more contrasty outlines, with halos.
How the photo\'s brightness is evened out inside the frame: how far highlights are dimmed, shadows lifted and layers of different exposure blended.
The way the scene\'s light is measured. Matrix weighs the whole frame, centre-weighted favours the centre, spot measures right at the focus point.
How light the photo comes out: the brightness auto-exposure aims for. Higher: lighter. Lower: darker. A shot with very bright places never gets darker than it was taken.

The floor below which the camera does not lower the exposure. Higher: frames in bright sun do not come out too dark. Lower: the camera may drop the exposure further for bright sunsets. A shot that includes short highlight frames never gets darker than it was taken.
How many times the camera may brighten a frame in the dark. Higher: dusk and night shots come out lighter. Lower: night shots are darker, but without extra noise and unnatural brightness.

How much clipping of bright sources the exposure allows. Lower: the camera guards the lights more strictly, dropping the exposure sooner for the texture of lamps and sky and lifting the shadows afterwards. Higher: bright lights shine more and the exposure is not lowered.

How strongly auto-exposure acts overall. Above 1 the brightness correction is stronger. Below 1 it is weaker and the photo stays closer to how it was taken. A shot that includes short highlight frames never gets darker than it was taken.

Keeps the brightness from being pushed at night as the sensor noise grows. Lower: the exposure is held back harder and the night stays dark and clean. Higher: brightness is pulled up in the dark even if noise comes with it.
Shifts the brightness of the data entering the processing, in stops. Leave 0 for normal shooting: auto-exposure brings part of the brightness back anyway.

The brightness above which the camera starts to compress and dim the highlights to save them from burning out. Lower: it dims them sooner and harder, keeping cloud and lamp detail but darker lights. Higher: the lights stay bright and contrasty, with more risk of clipping.

How much scene contrast it takes for the camera to lift the shadows by itself. Lower: shadows are lightened even in moderately contrasty scenes. Higher: only in very contrasty ones, such as against the sun; in ordinary shooting the shadows stay deep.
Which scenes the camera takes for dull and low in contrast: fog, an overcast sky. Higher: more scenes count as flat and get extra contrast more often. Lower: only really faded shots do.

How hard overexposed areas are darkened once the camera finds them. Higher: bright lamps and blown areas are dimmed more and show their texture. Lower: a gentle touch. At zero the lights are not compressed.
Extra contrast for dull and overcast shots. Higher: such a picture becomes deeper and more expressive. At zero the scene stays soft and flat as it is.
How hard the dark parts of the frame are pulled up. Higher: lighter shadows that show what the gloom hid. Lower: the shadows stay dark, contrasty and natural.

How hard blown areas are dimmed so that their detail shows. Higher: a bright sky, the sun and lamps are dimmed more and show relief. Lower: the lights stay bright and shining. When a shot includes short highlight frames, the strength comes from their real range and this value does almost nothing.
The weight of the second dark layer, between the highlight layer and the normal one. Higher: darker, more detailed bright places. Lower: brighter ones.

The weight of the darkest layer, the one in charge of the highlights. Higher: darker, more detailed lights. Lower: brighter ones. When a shot includes short highlight frames, half this weight is used.
The weight of the normally exposed layer. Higher: the photo stays closer to its original brightness. Lower: a stronger HDR effect.
The weight of the brightened layer, the one in charge of the shadows. Higher: lighter shadows. Lower: darker ones.
The gamma exponent of the output. Higher: lighter mid-tones and shadows, a flatter picture. Lower: darker and more contrasty.
Presses the black point down, as film does. Higher: the darkest shadows turn deep and velvety and the milky haze goes. At zero the shadows stay open and soft.
The photo\'s overall tone curve. AgX works by default; ACES, Uchimura or a curve you draw can replace it.
Ready variants of the AgX curve: neutral, punchy and contrasty, soft pastel, a warm film look. Custom takes the values of the rows below.
The slope of the middle of the AgX curve, the overall mid-tone contrast. Higher: more contrast. Lower: softer and flatter. Works in the Custom look.
Only for the OPPO Find X7 Ultra with the AgX look: the saturation with OPPO\'s colour matrix. Higher: brighter colours. Lower: paler ones.
Deep shadow softness (fusion and ACES toe)
How softly the darkest tones go to black. Higher: softer, lighter shadows with more detail in the gloom. Lower: deeper, more contrasty shadows. It works on every shot, with any curve.
The local contrast of medium-sized detail. It brings out the relief of objects, fabric and walls without oversharpening the fine stuff. Below zero the picture softens instead.
The contrast of the mid-tones round middle brightness. Higher: a fuller, more expressive picture with denser shadows and brighter lights. Lower: softer and more even.
The layer brightness the blend takes as best in our layout. Higher: a lighter photo. Lower: a darker one. When a shot includes short highlight frames, the centre is taken 0.15 higher.

How soft the borders are between areas of different exposure. Higher: wide, unnoticeable passages between light and dark zones. Lower: the layers blend more selectively and the HDR effect is stronger.

How large the zones are in which brightness is evened out, in pixels along the short side of the coarsest layer. Higher: the tone follows small zones and the picture is flatter. Lower: large zones, with more overall contrast.
Adds local contrast after the tone processing: textures look more expressive.
Rebuilds the true colour of blown highlights from the sensor channels that survived. Higher: tries harder to bring the colour back. Lower: a natural fade to white stays. Zero turns it off.
Highlights: trust threshold for surrounding colour
How coloured the light round a blown area may be for the blown area to take on its colour. Higher: the blown area is tinted. Lower: it stays whiter.
Removes the purple and green fringe round blown areas, contrasty branches and lamps. Higher: wide halos go too. Lower: only thin lines are cleaned. Zero turns it off.
Smooths the coloured dotted line on the edges of blown areas. Higher: stronger. Zero turns it off.

Blown white sources such as the sun, headlights and lamps, and the brightest zone round them, stay white without coloured rings, such as a yellow ring round the sun. Coloured sources keep their colour. Higher: stronger. Zero turns it off.
Cleans the short frames of noise before they go into the highlights. Higher: no colour sand inside bright lamps. Lower: small glowing lettering stays as sharp as possible. Zero turns it off.
A blown area fades smoothly to pure white, and coloured light to its own colour at full brightness. Higher: the transition starts sooner and is softer. Zero turns it off.
Bright coloured light such as LEDs and neon turns white. Higher: it whitens sooner. Lower: it keeps its colour longer. Zero turns it off.
Removes the coloured line on the dark side of contrasty edges. Higher: stronger. Zero turns it off.
Keeps sharpening from bringing out grain and noise on flat, even areas such as the sky, skin and walls. Higher: cleaner, but the finest texture is lost. Zero turns it off.
Removes colour noise in strongly lifted shadows. Higher: cleaner, but paler shadows; 0: off.
Colour vibrance: pastel and vivid, sky, greenery, highlights, mid-tones and shadows.
A smart colour boost: it enriches muted, calm hues and does not oversaturate ones that are already bright. Higher: calm tones come alive. Lower: a softer, more restrained palette.
The vibrance of blue sky and water. Higher: a deep blue or azure sky. Lower: the sky\'s colour is not pushed.
The vibrance of grass and leaves. Higher: fresh, lush greens that do not turn garish. Lower: a natural, restrained hue.
ES / L stamp on the photo
The photo\'s top right corner shows whether the extra-short (ES) and long (L) frames went into it, and if not, a short reason code.
Every shot keeps its raw burst in Download/SCAMERA so the merge can be examined. The files are large, up to several gigabytes a shot at 50 MP. Delete them once you have sent them.
Compares a shot with another value of a merge or processing setting. It needs saved raw bursts: turn on «Keep shots for the lab» inside.
Each SHDR shot keeps its RAW burst and parameters in Download/SCAMERA/Lab/<date_time> for the «Lab». The files are large (50 MP: up to a few GB a shot).
The system encoder saves the photo. That is about twice as fast, but the file is a little larger and the colour of fine detail is coarser.
Writes how long each stage of a shot takes to a file, to find what slows it down. The merge runs slower; the photo itself does not change.
Saves the processing\'s intermediate stages as a ZIP in Documents/SCAMERA/Dumps, separately from the log. It slows processing down and takes space.
The scam_dev.txt file changes these settings without the menu, with «key value» lines.
DCP colour matrices of the modules
The colour profile of this module: the camera\'s own or a loaded DCP file, a profile in Adobe\'s format. It changes how the camera renders colours.

The raw DNG file is compressed with no quality loss and takes about 40 percent less space. It saves a little slower, and not every app opens it.
Evens out the brightness of the frame\'s corners with the lens map. «Do not apply» is for a camera that already corrected the raw frame itself, when the corners come out too bright.
If the camera reports too high a black level, it is taken from the frame itself. Turn it on if the shadows of your photos look green.
Cropping the edges of the raw frame: the black stripes the camera delivers and your own margins on each side.
Shows how the frame is cropped on a portrait shot. You can drag an edge of the box with a finger.
If the raw frame has empty black stripes at its edges, they are cut off on every shot. That happens on the vivo X200 Pro and X200 Pro mini.
How many sensor pixels to cut from this side of a portrait shot, beyond the black stripes. Removes stripes and junk pixels at the frame\'s edge.

The form in which the camera delivers raw frames. Auto takes RAW10 when the camera offers it and the data fits 10 bits, otherwise 16 bit or RAW12. Change it only if photos come out with wrong brightness or colour.
Where the black and white levels come from: each frame\'s own data or the camera\'s fixed values.
Any chosen noise profile except Auto replaces the camera\'s data in the merge, the noise reduction, the frame alignment and the DNG.
Sounds, grid, focus, faces, HUD, horizon and theme
The shutter click and the timer sound, the self-timer\'s countdown. They sound only in the normal ring mode. Where the law requires a shutter sound, it is always there.
The click of a shot. It sounds only in the normal ring mode. Where the law requires a shutter sound, it is always there.
The self-timer\'s countdown beeps. They sound only in the normal ring mode.
The colour of chosen items, switches and the camera\'s buttons.
Photo format and quality, colour, Ultra HDR, 16:9, file name, watermark, settings backup
How hard the JPEG is compressed. Higher: a larger, more detailed file. Lower: a lighter file that loses fine detail.
Line text, icon, size and opacity
How large the watermark\'s text is, measured on the photo\'s short side: a portrait and a landscape photo get the same size. 7 is the default.
How solid the watermark is, its plate and frame included. 100 is opaque, lower is more transparent.
A config can be moved to another phone: the lens profiles are matched by focal length.

A 50 MP shot arrives already assembled into an ordinary frame by the sensor itself, as in the stock camera. Off: the camera takes the raw Quad or Tetra mosaic and assembles the frame itself. 200 MP is always assembled by SCAMERA: the sensor cannot do it. On the vivo X100 Ultra and X300 Ultra this applies to the main camera only.
For the Xiaomi 17 Ultra telephoto: from 3.2x to 4.3x the optics work, then a crop, and from 6.45x the in-sensor zoom. Off: the zoom works without these modes.
Root, package spoofing, diagnostics, log, developer options, about
Not required. Only a build in which the processor is not installed as part of the app needs it: then it starts through su.
The app\'s log, processing stages and reports, to look into a failure or an odd photo.
The camera sees another app name and opens hidden modules.
SCAMERA introduces itself to the camera as another app. It applies from the next time the camera opens.
OPPO and OnePlus open hidden cameras this way. The generic way changes the name inside the app. BinderHook is for experienced users. An empty field keeps the app\'s own name.
The format photos are saved in. JPEG opens everywhere. HEIC, WebP and AVIF take less space but do not open everywhere.
How hard the HEIC is compressed. Higher: a larger, more detailed file. Lower: a lighter file that loses fine detail.
10 bits a colour instead of 8: the sky and other smooth gradients come out without steps. Needs Android 13 or newer.
How hard the WebP is compressed. Higher: a larger, more detailed file. Lower: a lighter file that loses fine detail.
Saves every pixel without loss. The file is several times larger and takes longer to save. The quality slider does nothing then.
How hard the AVIF is compressed. Higher: a larger, more detailed file. Lower: a lighter file that loses fine detail.
Saves every pixel without loss. The file is about 6 times larger and takes longer to save.
How many bits a colour gets. 8 is as in JPEG. 10 gives smooth gradients without steps. 12 leaves room for later editing.
The resolution the colour is stored at. 4:4:4 keeps crisp colour edges. 4:2:0 makes the file smaller, with softer colour edges.
How fast an AVIF is saved. The slower, the slightly better the detail at the same file size.
sRGB looks the same on any screen. Display P3 holds richer colours: brighter on wide-colour screens, a little paler where P3 is not supported.
A brightness map is saved with the photo: Ultra HDR in JPEG or an HDR map in 10-bit HEIC and AVIF. On an HDR screen bright places glow brighter; on an ordinary one it is just a photo.
A JPEG copy is saved beside the HEIC, WebP or AVIF, for apps that cannot open those formats.
Finds faces in the frame, outlines them and puts focus and exposure on them. A tap on the screen and manual focus come first.
What the camera does when it finds a face in the frame: softer contrast, natural skin colour, separate processing of the face.
If the camera finds a face, the shot gets no extra contrast and the shadows on the face come out softer. Shots without faces do not change.

When the light has made skin clearly yellow or bluish and the grey and white things in the frame carry the same cast, the skin is brought back toward its natural colour. The background and normally coloured skin do not change.
How strongly the exposure adapts to the faces in the frame. Higher: faces are lit right even against the sun, though the background may get lighter. At zero faces do not affect the exposure.
White balance with an eye on the faces: the colour of the whole photo shifts so that skin gets closer to its natural tone. 0 is off, 1 is full strength. Small deviations are left alone.
When a face is found in the frame, the shot is processed with this curve and its modifiers instead of the usual one.
The tone curve for shots with faces. Soft by default, gentle on shadows. Tap to change it.
Separate processing of faces only: their brightness, contrast, colour, and the smoothing and sharpness of skin.
The brightness of faces, in stops. The rest of the photo does not change.
The contrast on faces, relative to the skin\'s own brightness.
How saturated the colour of faces is.
On the plus side faces are warmer, on the minus side cooler.
On the plus side faces are more magenta, on the minus side greener.
Removes the finest skin texture, pores and noise. At 100 the skin is as smooth as it gets.
On the plus side the fine detail of a face is sharper, on the minus side softer.
The size of the processed area relative to the face the camera found, in percent.
How strictly the mask follows skin colour. 0 is the whole oval of the face with hair and eyes, 100 is skin only.
For tuning: on the next shots the face mask is painted red so that you can see what it covers.
Turns on separate processing of faces: the rows below change faces only. Off: faces are processed like the rest of the photo.
How to start tracking: focus and exposure follow the chosen subject round the frame.
The photo goes through a model of film and print: colour, tone, grain and halation. The film\'s frame size changes the grain.
How strongly the LUT colours the photo. 0: not at all. 100: at full strength.
A tap places a focus ring and a brightness square that can be dragged separately. A tap on the ring returns to auto, a tap on the square moves it back to the ring.
The 2× grid is used only in good light and when the frames really add detail. Otherwise the shot is simply enlarged: faster and without grid traces.
The pattern new photos are named by. The line under the title shows the name of a photo taken now.
The strength of the unsharp mask\'s edge sharpening. Higher: a crisply sharp picture. Lower: a soft, natural image without oversharpening. Zero turns it off.
How much of the first stage\'s restored sharpness is mixed into the photo. Higher: clearly sharper. Zero turns it off.
How many passes the first stage makes. Higher: sharper, but slower and with possible halos. Lower: faster with less risk of noise. Zero turns it off.
How much of this stage\'s restored sharpness is mixed into the photo. Higher: sharper. Lower: softer. Zero turns it off.
How many passes this stage makes. Higher: stronger, but slower and with possible halos. Lower: weaker. Zero turns it off.
How much of this stage\'s restored sharpness is mixed into the photo. Higher: sharper. Lower: softer. Zero turns it off.
How many passes this stage makes. Higher: stronger, but slower and with possible halos. Lower: weaker. Zero turns it off.

How rounded the top of the curve is: how softly bright highlights roll into white. Higher: the lights stay bright longer and end more abruptly. Lower: they roll off more smoothly. Works in the Custom look.
How rounded the bottom of the curve is: how dark tones pass into black. Higher: denser, darker shadows. Lower: softer and lighter. Works in the Custom look.

The lower end of the AgX curve\'s range, in stops from middle grey. The lower it is, the more shadow detail stays and the flatter the picture. The higher, the sooner shadows go black. Works in the Custom look.
The upper end of the AgX curve\'s range, in stops. Higher: more room for highlights and less clipping, but a flatter picture. Lower: lights turn white sooner. Works in the Custom look.
How saturated the photo\'s colours are. Higher: richer. Lower: paler. At zero the photo is black and white.
Shifts the brightness before the AgX curve, in stops. Higher: a lighter photo. Lower: a darker one. Works in the Custom look.
The SCAMERA camera icon next to the text, with its light in the camera\'s yellow. On its own it is a watermark too.
Load settings from a saved file.
Return all settings to default. The app restarts.

How hard moving things are cut out where parts of the frame move differently. Higher: no doubling of passing people and cars at all, but a noisier shot. Lower: a gentler merge with less noise on things that sway slightly.
Deep night: colour denoise strength, 5 numbers small to large blotches. Higher: cleaner; lower: truer colour.
Night: colour denoise strength, 5 numbers small to large blotches. Higher: cleaner; lower: truer colour.
Dusk: colour denoise strength, 5 numbers small to large blotches. Higher: cleaner; lower: truer colour.
Dim light: colour denoise strength, 5 numbers small to large blotches. Higher: cleaner; lower: truer colour.
Save, restore or reset the settings
What the merge recorded about the last shot. Useful to look into a failure or an odd photo.
The camera screen\'s last 20 messages with their times and repeat counts. A long press on a message card opens the same.
Makes every shot warmer or cooler on top of the automatic white balance. At zero it is as the camera judged.
Shifts the photo\'s colour toward magenta or green on top of the automatic white balance, for example to remove a green cast from lamps. At zero it is as the camera judged.
Under incandescent lamps and at sunset part of the warmth stays in the photo instead of being removed by auto white balance. At zero the light is fully neutral.
In the shade and on overcast days part of the blue stays in the photo. At zero the light is fully neutral.
Keeps colour rich in the bright parts of the frame, such as sunsets and sunlit clouds. Higher: richer sunsets and glints. Lower: the lights are closer to neutral.
Makes skin redder or more golden; other colours do not change. Higher: more golden. Lower: redder. At zero as it is.
Evens out blotchy redness on skin by pulling its hues together. Higher: more even skin. Zero turns it off.
The hue, saturation and brightness of eight colours, each on its own.
Shifts this colour toward its neighbours on the colour wheel. At zero as it is.
Higher: this colour is richer. Lower: duller. At −100 it is grey.
Higher: this colour is lighter. Lower: darker. At zero as it is.
Tinting the shadows, mid-tones and highlights with a colour of their own, as in films.
The tint\'s colour on the colour wheel: 0 red, 60 yellow, 120 green, 180 cyan, 240 blue, 300 magenta.
How visible the tint is. At zero there is none.
Where shadows end and highlights begin. Higher: more of the photo counts as highlights. Lower: as shadows.
How smoothly the tinted zones blend into each other.
A colour filter for the black-and-white photo, as on black-and-white film. Yellow darkens the sky a little, orange and red more. Green lightens leaves, blue the sky.
Neon, LEDs and other very saturated colours keep their hue instead of turning into a flat patch. Higher: stronger protection. Zero turns it off.

Keeps the tone curve from distorting hues in bright places, such as pulling a blue sky to turquoise or violet and orange to yellow. Full holds every hue up to white, Blues only holds just the blues, Off leaves the colours as the curve makes them.
The hue and saturation of the camera\'s three primary colours: red, green and blue.
Turns this primary colour of the camera round the colour wheel, and with it every colour that contains it. At zero it is as the camera renders it.
Higher: this primary colour is richer. Lower: duller. At zero it is as the camera renders it. White stays white.
Turns on the ACES curve instead of AgX: deep contrast, softly compressed highlights. The other curves turn off.
The brightness of the signal entering the ACES curve. Higher: a brighter frame whose mid-tones fill sooner. Lower: a darker frame with more headroom.
How steeply brightness rises in the highlights of the ACES curve. Higher: brighter, livelier lights. Lower: a smooth, muted passage to the highlights.
The passage between mid-tones and shadows on the ACES curve. Higher: a softer passage and darker lights. Lower: harder mid-tone contrast.
Turns on the Uchimura curve instead of AgX, in the Gran Turismo style: even mid-tones, a soft highlight roll-off, adjustable shadows. The other curves turn off.
The brightness entering the Uchimura curve. Higher: the whole frame is lighter. Lower: darker.
The frame\'s final brightness after the Uchimura curve. Higher: everything is lighter, white included. Lower: a darker finished frame.
The ceiling of white on the Uchimura curve. Higher: brighter, harder lights. Lower: the brightest point is muted.
The contrast of the mid-tones. Higher: more contrasty, better separated mid-tones. Lower: a flatter, softer picture.
Where shadows end and mid-tones begin. Higher: a wider shadow zone. Lower: shorter shadows, the even mid-tones start lower.
How long the mid-tones run evenly before the highlights start to compress. Higher: a wider range of natural tones. Lower: the lights compress sooner.
How steeply the curve bends in its dark part. Higher: darker, more contrasty shadows. Lower: lighter shadows that show more.
Lifts the black level. Higher: a faded, matte black, as in old photos. At zero black stays clean and deep.
Turns on your own tone curve instead of AgX. It is set from −5 to +5 stops round middle grey. The other curves turn off.
Your tone curve. A tap adds a point, a drag moves it, a hold deletes it.
Merge frames, camera colour, RAW, viewfinder, diagnostics
The format photos are saved in and their quality. If unsure, leave JPEG.
How many pixels a photo has and what happens to it after the merge.
How much of the frame shows through the quick-settings panel. Text and icons always stay opaque.
The gallery\'s theme and its icon on the home screen.
Save every setting to a file, load them back, or reset them to how they were after installing.
The watermark on photos: its look, where it sits and what it shows.

The watermark with the current settings on a sample photo. It changes as soon as a setting does; the switch under it shows the photo in landscape or portrait. The values are a sample shot\'s: a real photo shows its own.

Caption: the icon and text right on the photo with a soft shadow. Badge: the same in a glass pill like the quick-settings panel. Bar: a glass band across the edge, the text on one side, the exposure on the other. Frame: a white or black border over the photo\'s edges with the text in its wider band; the photo keeps its size.

The corner or edge it sits on, as the photo is viewed: shot in portrait, landscape or upside down, it is always the right way up in that corner. A bar or frame takes the bottom or top edge; left and right choose the side of the text.

The text colour. Auto picks white or black by how bright the photo is under the watermark. A badge, bar or frame takes the opposite plate: dark glass or a black frame for white text, light ones for black text.
SCAM is the app\'s own font, the same on every phone. The others are the phone\'s condensed, serif and monospace fonts.
The distance from the photo\'s edges in percent of its short side. For a frame it is the border\'s width.
Shows the text of the row below. Off, the watermark has no text of its own.
The phone\'s model as the photo\'s EXIF records it.
The lens\'s focal length as a 35 mm equivalent (24mm), or its own when the equivalent is unknown.
When the photo was taken, in the format of the row below.
Date and time, the date only, the time only, year first, or the month as a word. Time is 24-hour.
Ready film colours. A LUT is a table that recolours the photo in the chosen style. This page shows what exactly it changes.
A soft glow round bright places, as from a glass filter in front of the lens: Glimmerglass, Black Pro-Mist, Pro-Mist, CineBloom.
Normal colour, black and white, or film: film colours, the film simulation and a lens filter.
Saves every setting into one file, a new profile.
Loads the settings from an .xml file in the SCAMERA folder. The current settings are replaced.
Puts every setting back as it was right after installing.
A shot with a crop or digital zoom is enlarged to the full photo size. Off: it stays smaller, without enlarging.
For full-resolution shots (50 and 200 MP) and in-sensor zoom, SCAMERA computes the white balance. Off: the camera\'s own white balance is used.

Film and paper profiles: spektrafilm by Andrea Volpato, github.com/andreavolpato/spektrafilm, CC BY-SA 4.0 (converted and modified by SCAMERA: binary arrays and derived LUTs, see assets/film/CHANGELOG.txt). The colour model, the DIR couplers and the diffusion filters are ports of spektrafilm (GPL-3.0); the 65 mm and IMAX 70 formats and the grain blur\'s format scale come from spektrafilm OFX by Aedan Diez, github.com/chaert-s/spektrafilm-ofx (GPL-3.0, see assets/film/NOTICE-spektrafilm-ofx.txt). Text recognition in the gallery: Tesseract OCR and its tessdata_fast models (Apache-2.0), github.com/tesseract-ocr, through Tesseract4Android by Adaptech (Apache-2.0).
Frames are taken brighter while the photo keeps its usual brightness, so the shadows have less noise. Indoors and at night it usually does nothing.

The order of groups and rows on the settings pages, as you like it. It is kept in the config.
How the camera chooses a photo\'s brightness: metering, protection of bright places, the shadow lift and the limits the exposure stays within.

The balance between saving detail in blown areas and the scene\'s usual brightness. Lower: highlight protection comes first, the frame is darker, sky and lamps hold. Higher: the frame\'s brightness comes first, the exposure drops less and bright sources may burn out.

How bright coloured things such as neon, a sunset or headlights go into clipping. At 100 percent they fade to white smoothly, as on film. Near zero colours in the lights stay harshly saturated and clip abruptly.
The layers of different brightness the photo is built from. Ours is the current way. Classic is four layers at −2.5, −1.2, 0 and +1.8 stops, with their own weights in the group below.
The share of the layer that compresses bright zones the most (−2.5 stops). Higher: detail returns in the brightest lights and glints. Lower: the natural glow stays. Works with the classic layout.

The share of the layer that compresses highlights moderately (−1.2 stops). Higher: the sky and light things keep their texture without losing overall contrast. Lower: the lights stay bright. Works with the classic layout.

How much the normally exposed layer matters. Higher: the picture stays closer to the original frame, without an HDR effect. Lower: the layers that lighten shadows and compress highlights weigh more. Works with the classic layout.
The share of the layer that lightens shadows (+1.8 stops). Higher: detail is pulled out of dark areas. Lower: the shadows stay deep and contrasty. Works with the classic layout.
The brightness the blend takes as ideal for a pixel. Higher: lighter layers are preferred and the frame is lighter. Lower: darker layers, a deeper frame. Works with the classic layout.
How the extra short frames for the highlights and long ones for the shadows are taken and merged.

Holds colour and detail in very bright lights such as neon, street lamps and the sun. At one signs keep their rich colour instead of burning into plain white. At zero it is off and the lights shine at full brightness.
The brightness above which lights start to be compressed. Higher: only the most blinding sources are touched. Lower: compression starts sooner and takes in every bright glint.
How bright the compressed lights may get. Higher: the lights stay bright and striking. Lower: they are pressed down harder and the colour of sign letters and lamp filaments shows better.
Recovering blown highlights and fighting the colour fringes and dotted lines at bright edges.
The base saturation of colours in the sensor\'s matrix. Higher: every colour is richer from the moment the raw frame is read. Lower: a restrained, muted palette. Brightness does not change.
Multi-level noise cleaning at three scales, fine grain and medium and large blotches, separately for brightness and colour. Off: only the main noise reduction is left.
How closely the denoiser\'s strength follows the sensor\'s noise on this shot. Higher: it cleans harder in low light and at high ISO. At zero it acts the same on every frame.
Cleans dark areas harder, where noise is worst. Higher: clean shadows without colour debris. At zero the strength is the same over the whole frame.
How hard grey grain is removed. Higher: smooth, even surfaces. Lower: texture and a little grain stay.
The finest, dot-like grain. Higher: fine sand goes from flat surfaces. Lower: the crispest hairs and pores.
Flaky medium-sized noise. Higher: cleaner at dusk. Lower: the natural micro-relief stays.
Large unevenness and waves of brightness in the dark. Higher: coarse blotches go from night shots. Lower: large gradients stay without smearing.
How hard coloured dots and blotches, green, purple and red, are removed. Higher: clean, even colours. Lower: colour is barely touched.
Lone coloured pixels. Higher: fine colour ripple goes. Lower: thin coloured threads and lines stay.
Medium colour blotches on walls and asphalt. Higher: colour smudges in the gloom go. Lower: natural colour transitions stay.
Large colour blotches in deep shadows. Higher: crimson and green patches in the corners of night shots go. Lower: the shades of night lighting stay.
Where frames were dropped because of motion, the edges of moving objects can turn jagged. This gives the base frame more weight and smooths such teeth. Zero is off, 4.5 is strong.
How strongly the geometric edges of objects are emphasised. Higher: architecture, lettering and crisp lines stand out more. Zero turns it off.
From which contrast an edge gets extra sharpening. Higher: only clear, crisp edges are boosted. Lower: even faint relief.
Removes thick, swollen outlines after strong sharpening. On the plus side thick lines become thin and neat. On the minus side sharp strokes are softened.
Holds the restoration back where the picture is already sharp, so that grain and rings do not grow. Higher: only real detail is boosted. At zero the filter works at full strength, but noise grows.
Holds the restoration back where the picture is already sharp: fewer rings and less noise. Zero turns it off.
Holds the restoration back where the picture is already sharp: fewer rings and less noise. Zero turns it off.
Smoothly lifts or lowers the mid-tones. The black and white points stay where they are.
An S-shaped contrast over the whole range: on the plus side shadows get darker and highlights lighter.
Changes the curve\'s steepness only in the shadows and dark mid-tones.
Changes the curve\'s steepness only in the bright tones and highlights.
Moves only the darkest shadows. On the plus side they lift, on the minus side they get deeper.
Moves only the brightest highlights. On the plus side they are muted, on the minus side they get lighter still.
Shifts the whole curve evenly up or down.
Adds contrast to your own curve in flat, low-contrast scenes, the way AgX does. Zero is off, one is the same as AgX.
Stronger filtering where the merge rejected frames (motion): x1.3 luma and x1.5 colour thresholds at 1. 0: off.
An extra boost for colours that are bright to begin with: clothes, flowers, signs. Higher: even richer. Lower: no garish tones.
The vibrance of the main subjects in the mid-tones. On the plus side everyday things look brighter, on the minus side the mid-tones are muted.
The vibrance of dark areas. On the plus side shadows are more colourful and warmer, on the minus side they lose colour and there is less colour noise in the gloom.

Keeps faces from turning red or carrot-coloured when you raise vibrance, the mixer or colour grading. At one the skin tone stays natural against any background, at zero skin is saturated along with the scene.
The hue the skin mask is built round, in degrees. Higher: the mask expects yellowish, peachy skin. Lower: pinkish red skin.
From which brightness an area may count as skin. Higher: the mask works only on well-lit parts of the face and does not catch warm things in the shade. Lower: it covers the face even in the gloom.
The saturation of faces only; the background stays. On the plus side faces look more tanned and rosy, on the minus side lighter and paler.
Shifts the skin\'s hue round the colour wheel, in degrees. On the minus side skin is pinker and rosier and yellowness goes. On the plus side warmer and more golden.
The red channel\'s factor in the colour matrix. Higher: more red, a warmer photo. Lower: less red.
The green channel\'s factor in the colour matrix. Higher: the photo shifts to green. Lower: to magenta.
The blue channel\'s factor in the colour matrix. Higher: more cold blue. Lower: a warmer photo.
The formula that turns the photo\'s brightness into screen brightness. Pure power is a plain gamma with dense shadows. sRGB and Rec.709 are the standards\' curves, with lighter, cleaner shadows.
Vibrance, skin tone, the colour matrix, white balance and the colour mixer.
How many pixels a «Static» photo gets. The frames of a still scene carry finer detail than one frame: 1.5× and 2× draw it out (super-resolution), at about four times the processing time.
How many refinement passes a «Static» photo gets. More: slightly finer detail and alignment, longer processing. Default 8.
Colour source, DCP profile, mosaic white balance, calibration
Everything about the shooting screen: corners, grid, horizon, the data over the frame and the RAW viewfinder.
The settings of shooting itself: Sport mode, HDR, shooting with less shadow noise, and focus.
How the app looks: the accent colour, the panel\'s transparency and the order of the settings.
A ready colour matrix for this sensor instead of the system one. Chosen separately for the module and for 50 and 200 MP shooting.
The colour is computed with the matrix of the row below, unless a ready profile is chosen. The matrix rows are scaled to sum to 1, so grey stays grey.
Nine numbers separated by commas, row after row. «1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1» changes nothing.
At high ISO the colour matrix is softened. There is less colour noise and the colours are a little calmer.
How far the colour matrix is softened by ISO 6400. At zero not at all, at one only the white balance is left.
Where a 50 or 200 MP shot takes its white balance from: the viewfinder at the moment of the press or its own estimate of the frame.
If the frame has deep shadows, the long frames are taken two stops brighter with a shutter of up to 1/60 s.
The number of long frames follows the share of shadows in the frame, from one to three. «Shadow frames: count» sets the most.
Everything about the module itself: the sensor, the RAW format, levels, the colour matrix and noise.
Camera2 keys of the session and of the requests, the sensor mode
Sensor, RAW, levels, colour matrix and noise
How far a dot\'s colour must differ from its neighbours to count as a defect. Lower: even faint stray dots are removed. Higher: only coarse ones.
How far a defective dot\'s colour is replaced with that of its surroundings. At one it is replaced completely; lower only weakens it. Brightness does not change.
Removes lone colour dots before the pyramid denoiser. Brightness does not change.
Source: Unspektrawesome by JohnTheFarm3r. Adaptation for SCAMERA. Tap to open the original project.
Sends the current app and error log as a text file.
The log is empty or storage is unavailable.
The camera adds short and long frames to keep detail in very bright and very dark places. Off: only ordinary frames are used, with fewer traces on motion and a slightly narrower brightness range.
Mid-frequency local contrast of the fusion. Higher: more structure.
Golden warms the AgX output and turns the hue lock off; the others change nothing by themselves.
Keeps blue skies from turning cyan near white.
The hue the skin mask centres on (degrees).
Rebuilds a clipped channel from the others near white. 0: off.
The tone of the “Oldstyle” camera mode: V1 the look of the old version 2.7, V2 of 3.1. Only the Oldstyle mode uses it; rows of the other version are greyed.

V1: two exposures of the frame through the 1024-point curve, blended by the 2.7 pyramid. V2: the RAW fusion of 3.1 with a short and a long gain and the 4096-point curve. Also on the “Tone” tile of the mode\'s adjustments.
M of the two virtual exposures\' gains (fusion_gains / maxDigitalGain): neither goes above it.
The 2.7 HDR\'s colour transfer onto its long exposure, with our merge as the reference: the colour of the shadows the 8-bit retone of the short exposure loses.
The 8-bit difference the transfer forgives per cell; a larger mean difference weakens it (motion rejection).
The supplement\'s haze and tint pass of the YUV route on our picture: the black point from the shadows\' histogram, the shadows\' colour cast pulled towards grey.
max_dark: the luma (0..255) the haze statistics look below.
The share of the frame (%) the black point keeps below it; 0.2 = 0.2 %.
corner_strength: how much of the shadows\' cast is pulled to grey; 0 keeps the colour.
The tint grid from our lens-shading gain map: stronger where the corners were lifted. Off: one value for the whole frame.
The supplement\'s output saturation on the finished picture: 0 neutral (the stage is skipped), plus more colour. The tone\'s own colour pass stays.
1 neutral; above 1 lifts the weak colours more than the strong ones.
Saturation added per stop of the picture\'s digital gain.
Vibrance added per stop of the picture\'s digital gain.
The colour output of 3.1 (its saturation_adjustment): 0 is its own look, plus more colour, minus less.
10 levels: the full frame of 3.1; 8: its postview, a little less local contrast at large scales.
